newsitem.title: UK: French EMU measures keep bond convergence alive.
newsitem.headline: French EMU measures keep bond convergence alive.

text.p: Deficit-cutting measures announced by the French government on Monday have removed one more obstacle to European currency union and ensured convergence trades remain firmly on track, analysts said.

The 32 billion francs ($5.3 billion) worth of deficit reductions outlined by Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn reaffirm the French commitment to European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) and keep the process on course for a January 1999 start, they added.
"If there had been significant disappointment, there would have been some unwinding of convergence trades," said Norman Williams, international economist at BZW in London.
"But as this was at least up to expectations, then the prospect for EMU -- and a broad EMU at that -- will remain on track."
Convergence trades speculate on the likelihood that the economies and financial instruments of EMU candidates will converge successfully.
Williams said the French measures were likely to prompt continued weakness of the mark and a further contraction in the yield spreads between peripheral bond markets and the core.

The audit of French public finances said the country's deficit to gross domestic product (GDP) ratio was running at 3.5 to 3.7 percent in 1997, above the three percent reference level stipulated in the Maastricht Treaty.
Strauss-Kahn said the government planned 22 billion francs in tax measures in 1997 and 10 billion francs of central government spending cuts, of which two billion would come from the defence budget.
The measures "concern 0.4 percent of GDP," he said.
Analysts said the measures announced by the government to tackle the overshoot were broadly in line with expectations, except for a higher than expected increase in corporation tax.

The French bond market gave the package a cautious welcome with the 10-year yield gap between French OATs and German Bunds swinging to minus 14 basis points (0.14 percentage point) after Strauss-Kahn's news conference from minus 11 before.
The package put France in no worse a situation than EMU partner Germany in terms of public finances and is likely to be enough to satisfy Chancellor Helmut Kohl for the time being, analysts said.
"There were no huge surprises in this but it does remove one more risk from the EMU process -- that France could mess it up," said Brian Venables, economist at ABN AMRO in Amsterdam.
He said the measures announced ensured EMU convergence trades would continue to squeeze the spreads between peripheral Europe and the core.
But he added a summer lull in trading would mean the Italian BTP/German Bund spread was likely to get stuck around the present one percentage point level for the time being.
Adrian Owens, European economist at Bank Julius Baer, said Italy and Spain were likely to be reassured by Monday's budget measures from France.

"Not only does it mean a timely start is likely but it also makes it much more difficult to exclude Italy or Spain...as they are likely to have a lower deficit this year than either France or Germany," he said.
"So ultimately I'm sure the BTP/Bund spread is going to go lower -- but there will be some near-term consolidation."
Owens predicted a BTP/Bund spread of 75 basis points by year-end. It was lately around 97 basis points, down from 99 at Monday's opening.
Analysts said the only sticking point in the French announcement was that Strauss-Kahn refused to specify a deficit target for 1997.
"The clear implication is a deficit to GDP ratio of around 3.25 percent this year...but the fact they're not giving a target in 1997 is a clear cop-out (evasion)," said Owens.
"The government is basically acknowledging it is not going to hit three percent."
"This is true to the EMU form -- another classic fudge," said Owens. "Not enough to thrill everybody but it's not going to derail the process." ($ = 6.041 French Francs)
